name: c-split-diptych
prompt: A tall portrait sheet of illustration board inked by hand in the manner of a front-page newspaper drawing from the year the Great War ended: black india ink laid over light graphite, lines that swell where the nib pressed and taper to hairs at their tips, tone built from crossing diagonal strokes that pack into solid black under the bench and inside the hat, and a faint ribbed texture of laid paper showing through the pale areas. A single thin inked rule, slightly wobbly as if pulled freehand along a ruler, divides the board into two stacked scenes of equal height, and between them lies a clean horizontal band of bare white board about a fifth of the sheet tall, nothing drawn in it. In the top scene, a gravel walk in a city park just after the armistice: bare elms, a gas lamp, a wrought-iron bench with slatted seat, seen straight on from a crouching height. On the bench's left end lounges a heavy, prosperous gentleman: jowls spilling over a winged collar, small clipped moustache, tall glossy silk topper, frock coat strained across a round belly, gold chain across the waistcoat, cane propped between his spats, his free hand lifted beside his ear with the palm turned out, brushing someone away, eyes half shut, chin tipped up. On the right end sits a gaunt young doughboy in a wrinkled khaki tunic, a single boot on the gravel and the other trouser leg pinned up short and empty below the thigh, a wooden crutch across his lap, overseas cap crumpled in his fist, leaning toward the gentleman as if to ask something. In the bottom scene, the very same bench from the very same spot, but the park is now: a steel litter bin, an LED lamp post, a parked hire bicycle, a glass office block rising behind the trees, all hatched in the identical ink. The gentleman is reproduced line for line, the same size, at the same place on the bench, the same lifted brushing hand, the same half-shut eyes and tipped chin, the same shine on the topper, so that his two figures stack one directly over the other like two pulls from one engraving. Beside him now slumps a worn-out night-shift nurse in loose scrubs and trainers, a lanyard at her neck, a paper cup going cold in her lap, turning toward him with the same hopeful lean the soldier had. Everything around him has changed; he has not changed by one line. Even, diffuse daylight with no cast shadows, pure black ink on off-white board, no colour, no grey wash. No writing anywhere in the picture: no words, letters, numbers, signature or speech balloons.
